fanoutqa_025055.x:
OPEC :: History and impact :: 1975–1980: Special Fund, now the OPEC Fund for International Development :: chunk_0009
Main article: [OPEC Fund for International Development](/wiki/OPEC_Fund_for_International_Development "OPEC Fund for International Development")

OPEC's [international aid](/wiki/International_aid "International aid") activities date from well before the 1973–1974 oil price surge. For example, the [Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development](/wiki/Kuwait_Fund_for_Arab_Economic_Development "Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development") has operated since 1961.[[73]](#cite_note-73)

In the years after 1973, as an example of so-called "[checkbook diplomacy](/wiki/Checkbook_diplomacy "Checkbook diplomacy")", certain Arab nations have been among the world's largest providers of foreign aid,[[74]](#cite_note-74)[[75]](#cite_note-75) and OPEC added to its goals the selling of oil for the socio-economic growth of poorer nations. The OPEC Special Fund was conceived in [Algiers, Algeria](/wiki/Algiers,_Algeria "Algiers, Algeria"), in March 1975, and was established in January 1976.[[76]](#cite_note-76)

"A Solemn Declaration 'reaffirmed the natural solidarity which unites OPEC countries with other developing countries in their struggle to overcome underdevelopment,' and called for measures to strengthen cooperation between these countries... [The OPEC Special Fund's] resources are additional to those already made available by OPEC states through a number of bilateral and multilateral channels."[[77]](#cite_note-77) The Fund became an official international development agency in May 1980 and was renamed the [OPEC Fund for International Development](/wiki/OPEC_Fund_for_International_Development "OPEC Fund for International Development"),[[78]](#cite_note-78) with Permanent Observer status at the United Nations.[[79]](#cite_note-79) In 2020, the institution ceased using the abbreviation OFID.

fanoutqa_017375.x:
Diébédo Francis Kéré :: Early life and education :: chunk_0001
Kéré was born in the village of [Gando, Burkina Faso](/wiki/Gando,_Burkina_Faso "Gando, Burkina Faso"). He was the first child in the village to be sent to school as his father, the village chief, wanted his eldest son to learn how to read and translate his letters. Since no school existed in Gando, Kéré had to leave his family when he was 7 years old to live with his uncle in the city. After finishing his education, he became a carpenter and received a scholarship from the [Carl Duisberg Society](/wiki/Carl_Duisberg#Carl_Duisberg_Society "Carl Duisberg") to do an apprenticeship in Germany as a supervisor in [development aid](/wiki/Development_aid "Development aid"). After completing the apprenticeship, he went on to study architecture at [Technische Universität Berlin](/wiki/Technische_Universit%C3%A4t_Berlin "Technische Universität Berlin"), graduating in 2004.[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5)

During his studies he felt it was his duty to contribute to his family and to the community which had supported him, and to give the next generation the opportunity to follow in his footsteps. In 1998, with the help of his friends, Kéré set up the association Schulbausteine für Gando e.V. (now Kéré Foundation), which loosely translates as "Building Blocks for Gando", to fund the construction of a primary school for his village. His objective was to combine the knowledge he had gained in Europe, with traditional building methods from [Burkina Faso](/wiki/Burkina_Faso "Burkina Faso"). He completed his studies and built the first school in Gando as his diploma project in 2004, while also opening his own architectural office Kéré Architecture.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-:3-11)

Kéré is known for involving community in his projects and for his innovative use of [vernacular](/wiki/Vernacular_architecture "Vernacular architecture") materials and techniques.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[11]](#cite_note-:3-11)

Established in 1811, Brown's Alpert Medical School is the fourth oldest medical school in the Ivy League.[[12]](#cite_note-:13-13)[[h]](#cite_note-146)

In 1827, medical instruction was suspended by President [Francis Wayland](/wiki/Francis_Wayland "Francis Wayland") after the program's faculty declined to follow a new policy requiring students to live on campus. The program was reorganized in 1972; the first M.D. degrees from the new Program in Medicine were awarded to a graduating class of 58 students in 1975. In 1991, the school was officially renamed the Brown University School of Medicine, then renamed once more to Brown Medical School in October 2000.[[139]](#cite_note-147) In January 2007, entrepreneur and philanthropist [Warren Alpert](/wiki/Warren_Alpert "Warren Alpert") donated $100 million to the school. In recognition of the gift, the school's name was changed to the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University.

In 2020, *[U.S. News & World Report](/wiki/U.S._News_%26_World_Report "U.S. News & World Report")* ranked Brown's medical school the 9th most selective in the country, with an acceptance rate of 2.8%.[[140]](#cite_note-usnews.com-148) *U.S. News* ranks the school 38th for research and 35th for primary care.[[141]](#cite_note-149)

It officially became a university in 1896 and was subsequently renamed Princeton University.

The university is governed by the [Trustees of Princeton University](/wiki/Trustees_of_Princeton_University "Trustees of Princeton University") and has an endowment of $37.7 billion, the largest [endowment per student](/wiki/List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_the_United_States_by_endowment "List of colleges and universities in the United States by endowment") in the United States. The [Karaiskakis Stadium](/wiki/Karaiskakis_Stadium "Karaiskakis Stadium") in [Piraeus](/wiki/Piraeus "Piraeus"), the home ground of Greece from 2004 until 2017, and again since 2024.

Traditionally, Greece has spent most of its history playing home matches in different stadiums primarily in or near [Athens](/wiki/Athens "Athens"), as well as in various other cities across the country. The national team's home ground was the [Karaiskakis Stadium](/wiki/Karaiskakis_Stadium "Karaiskakis Stadium") in [Piraeus](/wiki/Piraeus "Piraeus") from its reconstruction in 2004 until 2017.[[64]](#cite_note-64)

Since their first international fixture in 1929 and for the next 33 years, Greece regularly used the [Leoforos Alexandras Stadium](/wiki/Leoforos_Alexandras_Stadium "Leoforos Alexandras Stadium") as their home ground. Their first home match away from it was played at the [Nikos Goumas Stadium](/wiki/Nikos_Goumas_Stadium "Nikos Goumas Stadium") in 1962, and the Karaiskakis Stadium was used for the first time in 1964 after it was renovated. In 1966, [Kaftanzoglio Stadium](/wiki/Kaftanzoglio_Stadium "Kaftanzoglio Stadium") in [Thessaloniki](/wiki/Thessaloniki "Thessaloniki") became the first venue outside Athens to host the national team. From then on, these stadiums were alternated until the early 1980s, along with others like Thessaloniki's [Toumba Stadium](/wiki/Toumba_Stadium "Toumba Stadium") and [Kleanthis Vikelidis Stadium](/wiki/Kleanthis_Vikelidis_Stadium "Kleanthis Vikelidis Stadium"), inaugurated in 1975 and 1977, respectively. Greece also played home matches at other venues such as [Kostas Davourlis Stadium](/wiki/Kostas_Davourlis_Stadium "Kostas Davourlis Stadium") in [Patras](/wiki/Patras "Patras") and [Anthi Karagianni Stadium](/wiki/Anthi_Karagianni_Stadium "Anthi Karagianni Stadium") in [Kavala](/wiki/Kavala "Kavala") during the 1970s. *Oppenheimer* grossed $330.1 million in the United States and Canada and $645.7 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $975.8 million;[[6]](#cite_note-BOM-6)[[7]](#cite_note-NUM-7) $190 million of which came from IMAX alone.[[181]](#cite_note-182) It is the [third-highest-grossing R-rated film](/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_R-rated_films "List of highest-grossing R-rated films") of all time behind *[Joker](/wiki/Joker_(2019_film) "Joker (2019 film)")* (2019) and *[Deadpool & Wolverine](/wiki/Deadpool_%26_Wolverine "Deadpool & Wolverine")* (2024).[[182]](#cite_note-183)[[183]](#cite_note-184) In September 2023, *Oppenheimer* became the highest-grossing biographical film of all time, surpassing [*Bohemian Rhapsody*](/wiki/Bohemian_Rhapsody_(film) "Bohemian Rhapsody (film)") (2018).[[184]](#cite_note-185)[[185]](#cite_note-186)

By August 2023, *Oppenheimer* had become the highest-grossing film ever to not reach the top spot at the domestic box office, although in its sixth weekend it topped the worldwide box office with a total of $38.12 million, surpassing *Barbie* for the first time.[[186]](#cite_note-187) It is also the highest grossing World War II-related film, surpassing *[Dunkirk](/wiki/Dunkirk_(2017_film) "Dunkirk (2017 film)")* (2017), also a Nolan film.[[187]](#cite_note-188)[[188]](#cite_note-189) Additionally, *Oppenheimer* became one of the top five highest-grossing IMAX releases, earning $183 million[[189]](#cite_note-rerelease-190) (approximately 20% of its total gross), over $17 million of which was earned from the 30 screens showing IMAX 70 mm prints.[[190]](#cite_note-191) The film was booked to be rereleased in IMAX theaters on November 3, including six IMAX 70 mm prints, as these theaters reported selling out during the initial release.[[189]](#cite_note-rerelease-190) *[Deadline Hollywood](/wiki/Deadline_Hollywood "Deadline Hollywood")* calculated the net profit of the film to be $201.9 million, when factoring together all expenses and revenues.[[191]](#cite_note-192)
